long before the doctors did. Some inaudible voice whispered the date and time, sometimes plainly, sometimes in a sing-song voice. So with both hands stuffed in his pockets, he would walk the lane towards the bus each morning, whistling some old song that no one alive could quite remember. He'd sit on the bus with his briefcase on his lap, making idle conversation with whoever happened to be near.

Randall Redman took it well, the doctor concluded, replaying that day in his mind as he drove home. Inoperable, but with treatment they might squeeze six more months out. Randall Redman waved his hand and shook his head at that idea. Like he was shooing some fly away. Without treatment, he doubted Randall would be around for six weeks, let alone six months. Randall smiled, liked he'd heard that argument before. He shook his head again, put on his hat, and walked home.

Randall Redman woke up crying from the dream. His hand searched wildly for the light until he found it. He went out to kitchen, and poured himself some water and stood by the window, waiting for the sun to come up. Today was the day. The bus would be arriving in fifteen minutes. He checked his watch, picked up his briefcase and walked out the door. He didn't look back.

Randall Redman didn't make it to work that day, or any day after for that matter. People at the office began to worry, and the police were notified. They found no record of a Randall Redman, and the address he had listed was actually the home of an older couple, who had no idea about any of it. It puzzled the police officers for about a week, and then, they too forgot.

Three states away, Randall Redman stood outside an all-night convenience store, his hand clutching something in his pocket. The sharp flourescent lights made him feel ill, even from the parking lot. He waited for the right moment. He saw the cashier's hands fly up, and he heard yelling. He swallowed hard, and walked inside. He didn't look back.
Randall Redman knew that he was dying,
